If a slip of zinc he applied to the tip of the tongue, and a silver coin placed between the gum and upper lip he brought into contact. an acid taste is experienced ; hut if the position of the metals tie reversed, the taste is theu decidedly alkaline. In order to (tie production of these sensations, the tongue must he covered with some moisture, for when perfectly dry, no such impressions are perceived. lion. Agents have been despatched to the colonies, to study the question of slavery and its incidents on the spot. Amongst these, M. Jules Le Chevnllier distinguished himself by his researches, and nu elaborate report, Committees of peers and deputies have discussed the subject, deliberated upon projects, and reported luminously, ns the report drawn up by that enlightened statesman the Due de Broglie, will exemplify. The solution, however, has yet to come, although doubtless, the public and Colonial mind must have been healthily maturing lor the inevitable conclusion. M. Gustave de Molinari, in a recent well written publication, has conceived a plan by which he purposes to reconcile all interests, whilst accomplishing every desirable object. Opinions will differ ns to the feasibility of the plan, and the practicability of t lie details, for working out which an expensive and complicated machinery would he required, upon, however, the seif supporting principle as far as possible. The difficulties in tins respect would appear to he insuperable. The ingenious and plausibly devised schemes is, however, well deserving notice, not only for the philanthropy of the sentiment by which it was prompted, but for the curious and clever calculations with which it is illustrated. The principal features of it are as follows : þÿ þÿ Our four colonies, Guadeloupe. Martinique, Guiana, and Bourbon, contain 200,000 slaves, whose labour is equivalent to that of 100.000 effective workmen ; 200 slaves, on

i ho average, not doing more than 80 free laborers. þÿ Again 200 negroes cost, per annum, 30.000 francs, the 200,000 negroes, therefore 30 millions. þÿ It is known, moreover, that a slave generation produces to the Antilles from 7 to 7$ years of labour. So that for 7 times and a half the labour of 200 000 slaves, or suv 2 milliards 340 millions of hours of effective work, the slaves expend 192j millions francs. M de .Mol iua t i proposes, therefore to expropriate the planters from the property in their slaves, and to furnish them in seven years and a half with the two milliards and 8 10 millions of effective working hours in return for their 292 j millions of francs of expenditure. The government he suggests, by the means of special agents, shall take an account of the weekly demand for labour by the colonist, and hire in Asia, or in India, where men superabound, the requisite number of labourers An account to he opened with each planter, who will lie debited with all the hours of work done, and credited with all the sums paid. On the expiration of the seven and a half years, the accounts to be balanced, the slave generation to be ransomed, and then the planters to pay the wages of the workmen themselves. It is to he understood that the negroes become free, may hire themselves out or cultivate a plot on their own account, or option to go to the British West India Colonics, where they may obtain wages which range from 1 francs to 2 francs per þÿday. M. de Molinari has, besides, a more spe-

cious than realizable conception for extract' ing from the imported fieo labourer from India, or Chinn, the cost of his passage. He would have the total cost entered upon a cortificalc to be given him, and a rateable sunt veaily deducted from biswages to dear it oil, in a term, say five years. Moreover he

b i AT18 would insure the lives of the free laborers for tbt; terms, debiting them with the etiarge of assurance. And after all deductions oil this ground and otheis, fie considers they would still gain ten times more wages than a Chinese labourer at Canton. þÿ Palladium

from the New York Commercial Advertiser, August 15, 1810. Potatoes. þÿ The potatoc is one of the tnost important vegetables known in the temperate zone. In some countries it constitutes a large portion of the food of the inhabitants, and may be reckoned among the ttecessaiies of life þÿ a vegetable for whose various excellent qualities no substitute can be found. It is therefore not wonderful that the mysterious disease, which has proved so destructive to this root in all parts of the World for the past two years, should excite great regret and alarm þÿ and that the character of the disease should be investigated, and attempts made to discover means for preventing the decay of this vegetable But although many prominent men interested in the noble business of agriculture have turned their attention to this subject, have carefully examined all the facts, and framed various learned and ingenious theories, yet we believe nothing has yet appeared which is calculated to throw any light on the mysterious nature. of the disease, which seems the present year to be extending its ravages þÿ and is destructive indeed. According to present appearances, there will be but very few, if any, potatoes taised the present season, for Winter stock. We learn that the disease has already shown ilselt in its worst form in mauy vegetable gardens in this vicinity, where it never appeared before--and its effects arc becoming more visible and destructive every day, i insomuch that it can haidlv he expected any sound potatoes can be found in the hills alter

the lapse of a few weeks This is a serious misfortune, although the prospect is favourable for a large crop of grain, and it behooves our leading agricultuiists to be looking about for a substitute, þÿ It is well known that in the West Indies, 'and other places in Southern latitudes, there are many nutritive and highly palatable esculent vegetables, besides several vaiielies ol the vain, a vegetable, which cannot probably lie raised in tfiis climate. If some public spirited individual would make an exploring tour for t his purpose to the West India Islands, and succeed in discovering a good substitute for the potato, which would flourish in our climate, he would indeed be a benefactor to the human race. þÿ Potatoes constitute the ground work of a good dinner throughout all chrisliandnm and, in many places, were the potatoes taken trom the table and no substitute provided, there would be but little left 10 satisfy the appetite uf a hungry man. Neapolitan Aquatics þÿ There arecertuin aquatic amus menls practised by the Neapolitans in the Bay, which ate peculiar to that locality. As 1 do not remember hav ing seen such exhibitions any where described 1 may shortly allude to them. One ol them is a tournament, in which the rival forces consist of twelve boats on each side, respectively painted red and blue; they are very small, probably about ten feet long, and are each manned by two men. One pulls the boat ; the other the champion, stands upon a platform raised flush with the sides of the boat at iis stern; these ate armed with very long wooden lances, on the end of which is a leathern ball. At a given signal a boat fioin each of the opposing ranks gulls out; and meeting mid way, the two warriors level their lanceR, and coming in direct collision, one, and sometimes both, are precipitated into the sea ; the boats immediately pull back again into position, leaving the discomfited knight to pick up his lance and fidlow at his leisure In this way the fight continues till one side (or colour of bout)

has every man immersed Victory, then, as to the colour, is decided. It sometimes happens, however, two of one coiotu ate left; and these contend again for the individual prize. These being the most dexiions, often sustain each other's shocks six or seven times) till at length one is precipitated into the sea. and thus ends the fight Another species ol amusement consists in placing a purse of money at the outer end of the bowsprit of a ship; the said bowsprit being well grea»ed, and considerably inclined upwards. The puise becomes the property of the first man who can take it. The individuals who make the attempt run up the bowspiit in ail variety of ways. Some of them set out as fast as they can ; others warily and slowly ; but as long as 1 looked on, none succeeded in reaching tfie purse; they invaiiably fell into the sea, and, swimming to the ship, ascended its side, and were ready again foi another attempt. J lie bowsprit is of course, disencumbered of all its cordage for tfie occasion. The only risk which an individual runs in practising this amusenu nt, is in not being aide to get away from under the bowsprit before his next neighbour tumbles above him; in which case, as the height is considerable, the paities coining into contact are sometimes much hurl ; and the keenness exhibited is so gieat that theie are often two individuals on the beam at the same time. There is no fear of dtowuing. All around t tie Bay of Maples the natives in their yi<ulh li e more in the water than on

land ; indeed they spend the whole day Iving naked on the shore and sporting in die sea ; they are perfectly amphibious; and the only way to drown a Neapolitan would he to tie a twenty four pound shot to Ins neck.

Be prudent in the thought of diess, Bo sparing of thy parties ; Where fashion tiots in excess, O! nothing there of heart is: And can its palling sweets compare With love of faithful bosom ! Then of the faithless tree beware, There's poison in its blossom !

Bear and fo bear, for much thou'lt find in married life to tease ve, And should thv husband seem unkind, Averse to smile or please ye. Think that amid the cares of life His troubles fret and tease him : Then smile as ii becomes a wife, And labor well to ease him.

Aye, answi r him with loving word: Be each tone kindly spoken. For sometimes is the holy chord Bv angry jarring broken. Then curb thy temper in us rage, And fiet.ful be thou never; For broken once a t'eaiful change Frowns over both for ever.

Upon thy neck light hang the chain, For Hymen now hath bound ye, O'er thee and thine tnny pleasure reign, And smiling h mints surround ye, Then fare ye well, and may each lime The sun smiles, and yc wiser: Pray kindly take ihe well meant rhyme Of thy sincere adviser. We dotihly feel ourselves alone, Something, iny friend, We yet may gain There is a pleasure in litis pain: It soothes tin love ol lonely rest, ' Deep in its gentler hen it impressed. l is silent amid worldly toils. And stifled soon by mental broils; But. in a bosom thus prepared lis still small voice is ohen heard, Whispering a mingled sentiment, 'Twixt resignation and content. Oft in my mind such thoughts awake Bv lone St. Mary's silent lake; Thou know'st it well þÿ nor (en, nor sedge, Pollute the pure lake's crystal edge; Abrupt and sheer, the mountains sink At once upon the level brink ; And just a trace of silver sand Marks where the water meets the land. Far in the mirror, bright and blue, Each hill's huge outline you may view ; Shaggy with heath, but lonely bare, Nor tree, nor bush, nor brake is there, Save where, of land, yon slender line Bears thwart the lake the scattered pine. Yet even this nakedness has power, And aids the feeling of the hour: Nor thicket, dell, nor copse you spy, Where living thing concealed might lie; Nor point, retiring, hides a dell, Where swain, or woodman lone, might dwell; There's nothing left to fancy's guess, You see that all is loneliness : And silence aids þÿ though these steep hills Send to the lake a thousand rills ; In summer tide, so soft they weep, 'The sound but lulls the ear asleep; Your horse's hoof tread sounds too rude, So stilly is the solitude. þÿ OOO- THE LADIES PORT- FOLIO.

(From the Matamoras Flag.) Monterey. As the Army of occupation has commenced its advance upon the interior of Mexico, by pursuing the Kio Grande upas high as Camargo, both by land and water, and as this will he the place where a permanent depot will he established and from which the advancing armv will leave the Kio Grande when it takes tip its general march upon Monterey, it will naturally hold a conspicuous place in the estimation of the American people þÿ Camargo is situated immediately upon the banks of le San Juan river, three miles from its junction with the Kio Grande. It is a sinull rudely constructed village, wiih some lew stone buildings, many buiil of mud

bticks dried in tlie sun. some cons' noted by driving stakes into the ground, and then plastering them with mud, and otutis loaned of cane and plastered in like manner. 'The number of inhabitants will not exceed two thousand; hut as the Mexican government has never thought her population worthy of enumeration, no positive statement can be made of the population of at y of their towns. The late extraordinary use of the Kio Grande has caused the San Juan to back op and literally inundate Camargo, to the great damage ol houses and other property ; also lo the sacrifice of several lues. Camargo may he considered as the head of navigation, for above, the bed of the tiver is so fi led up with rocks, tiiat its navigation higher up has never been attempted. The road upon leaving Camargo and crossing the San Juan becomes higher and less obstructed hv swampy grounds, and it then becomes an important enquiry what other obstacles may present themselves in the distance between this place and Monterey, which is 210 miles. The road passes through a level country, thieklv set with a small undeiwood, the largest timber being the ebony and the musquito, neither of which grow to the height of more than 12 or 15 feet and 12 to 14 inches in diameter. So dense is this underwood, that armies of 10.000 men each might march for half a day within a mile of eac.lt other, without the vicinity of one lo the other being known. The literal meaning of Monterey is the King's woods: but to those that have been

raised in a heavily timbered country, it would he moie appropriate to term it a grove of bush. It is a common saying with Texans who have travelled through the forest that ' it's so d þÿ d thick you can't shove a bowie knife into it." And what may appear somewhat singular, every buslt and shrub is armed with thorns curved in the shape of fish hooks, and the hold they take on the clothes and skin of travellers is not easily shaken oil. as the jackets of the soldiery will testily before they teach Monterey, The whole distance is well watered from Augusluntil March, plenty of wood f reasonable pasture, many herds of cattle, numerous flocks of sheep arid goats, now and then a small village þÿ which all have the npprarance of decay. Scattered along the road are miserable little huts, singularly picturesque from their original construction, not quite equal to rail pen stables built in the backwoods of Arkansas and Texas for scrub ponies. Yet Nature, in her mighty formations, has formed some positions on this road which if taken advantage of by a skiTuI and daring enemy, would prove a second Thermopylae to those who might have the temerity to tread those formidable passes. 'The American army will no doubt look ahead before entering these dangerous and shady pavilions. The mazes of the labyrinth are beautifully pictured out by meandring path's and conflicting cross roads, leading to the farmer's tiut, some watering place, or the wily lure of some Mexican bandit. When in fifteen leagues of Monterey the

village of Calderclte presents itself, enjoying the most lovely station, standing upon a perfectly level plain, surrounded with green grovel, presenting everlasting summer, the fields blessed with natural fertiiiry. The beholdei involuntarily exclaims, Why should a Mexican toil or labour I

n Ii is not indispensable that ihe army should pass through Caiderette, as there are other roads by which Monterey can be approached, but We mention this route as supplies can be obtained in Calderette, and the direction is nearest a straight lino. Immediately on leaving this place you enter again those shady, winding pavilions, and continue in them until you arrive within sight of Monterey. Many little streams and rivulets intersect the road, and some muddy lanes winch at times become impassable, so that the army will he fortunate if able to proceed in files of six deep ; but as the near vicinity to Monterey is somewhat opened a digression might be made to the right, and intersect the road that comes from the mouth of el Canon de Salinas, it being the most open road of the two. The creek that washes the southeast side of Monterey runs between these two roads, the fields forming a border on either side. The road that leads from Cal derette, when within a mile of Monterey, has the appearance of a small village, the houses being so numerous. Passing through tins seeming village, and arriving upon the bank of the creek, you have Monterey in view on the opposite side, presenting a very handsome appearance. The city is regularly laid out, the streets, avenues, and squares are shaded with numerous fruit and other trees, ami the houses generally exhibiting much taste and regularity in their construction. The city is well watered, and every thing about it strikes the beholder as grand and

beautiful. A passing view of the city would convey the idea of a large population, but a close inspection of its castle like edifices, sometimes occupying a whole square, sheltering hut the members and servants of a single fatnilv: therefore, from observation, we should not give the city a population of trvre than ti.HOO souls, and it is doubtful Whether it is even so great. Cast the eye beyond Monterey, and the sublime presents itself in lofty upreared pyramids of adamantine Stone, tinged with a crimson red, where the creeping vine cannot be found, and where the cedar and the pine children of the Alpine heights ; have never dared to rear their heads þÿ the sides and summits of these vast mountains presenting nothing to view but the bare and glitteiing stone ; but in whose bosom lie concealed beds of pure silver, and spaikltng beds of virgin gold. In the midway distance rise numerous ta lc mounds, commanding the town and all the entrances from Ihe Northeast. Upon one of these commanding positions the devoted people endeavored to raise a temple or dwelling for their bishop, hot their Zeal was greater than their means, and Ihe structure remains unfinished. If the Mexicans could withstand the double dealing havoc of an American charge, here might they plant the colours of their unfortunate country, and reap some of the laurels awarded to l.eoni das, or perhaps faintly pourlray in miniature the daz/.ling chivalry of those devoted heroes wtio fell battling on the ramparts ol the ever

A friend recommends the loilowing very simple, hut efficacious method for teliefin such cases; and having seen us operation, we present it to our readuis. Should the obstruction be in the vpper part of the eye, take the eyelashes ol the upper lid between the lingers of one hand, and draw it away Irom the eye ball, while with the other band, piess the lower row of eyelashes completely underneath, (between the eye ball and the upper ltd.) closing the eye firmly, at the same instant. A little gentle working to atid fro, of the eyelid, with the linger thus thoroughly hipped over each other þÿ will immediately remove the obstruction. Should the cinder have lodged in the lower part of the eye, place the upper row of eyelashes in the same position, underneath the lower part of the lid (us described above,) and the relief is certain. THE LATE EARTHQUAKE IN TUSCANY. M. Pilla, professor of geology at the University of Pisa, has published an iiiteiesiing account of the circumstances attendant on the late earthquake in Tuscany. We select from this work the following description of the earthquake at Pisa: þÿ " Oil the 14ih the weather at Pisa was as serene as on several preceding days. At noon 1 was as usual in the Museum of Natural History of the University, when I observed to some one near me, The air to day really seems about to catch fire.' Never was a prophecy so quickly realised. At a few minutes before one o'elock the Atmosphere was perfectly calm, when 1 heard a noise, which came rapidly from the side of ihe marine on the west. The impression 1 first felt was that of a violent wind advancing towards the town ; Itiut reflecting oil the impossibility of such a phenomenon arising so rapidly in the midst of the previous calm, I began to dread a disaster. M v suspicions were soon verified. The noise advanced witli still increasing force, and suddenly the salle, where I happened to he, began to tremble; to the vibration succeeded a violent agitation in a horizontal direction, with a dreadful noise. Accustomed to these phenomena, which are not rare in try country (.VI. Piltn is a Neapolitan). I ran to one of the windows, which ojiens on the garden of a neighbouring house, and tticie witnessed a most terrible spectacle 'I ho houses around were agitated in the most frightful manner; the trees in the garden,

by their motion, announced the violent agitation of the atmosphere ; these movements, added to those of the salle in which 1 stood, produced such a swimming in the head, that I was compelled to hold fast by the windows. The agitation continued, evidently iri a horizontal direction, backward and forward, but with extreme violence. In this dicadful situation the ceiling of the sollc began to fall on me ; and the cries which proceeded from the neighbouring houses added to the horror of the scene Atone moment I thought the town was about to be swallowed up Then, impelled by an instinctive feeling, I mounted on the window to leap into the garden ; but a momentary reflection restrained me; and by degree the ground again became quite tranquil '1 he shock once over, I left the .Museum, and found the streets filled with fteoplc, whose countenances expressed tlie utmost tenor. Every where reigned that silence with which Tacitus represents nun to be seized when ugiiated by any deep feeling in common, Aftei acquiring 'he ccrti'orlo that those most þÿ dear to inc wete safe, nu first thought was

for the leaning tower. I ran to see what had b come of it, and great was my surprise at finding it still standing, and firm. What an object it must have formed at the moment of the shock ! Those who had the opportunity of observing it at the moment assured me that its vibrations were most nWf'ul. But before inquiring into the effects, let us state what were its direction and duration. The first movement was manifestly vibratory ; after this came a violent undulating agitation which lasted till the end of the shock, except that the motion became slightly weaker towards the middle of the shock, and at the end doubly stronger. Its horizontal direction was the salvation of Pisa. If the vertical movements had been attended with the same intensity, the effects would have been more disastrous." þÿ London Paper Sept 14.

The Englishman was so lucky as to win the first fire and so unlucky as to miss his adversary. a o 'i a TJ ' Stop, stop 5 I'll huv your shot " The first impression made was that of the novelty of the proposal; the second, that it contained the preliminaries of a mutually profitable transaction. Singular Adventure. þÿ We understand that an accident of a very singular description occurred to one of our fellow citizens when recently bathing al Aidentinny. The gentleman in question, while swimming at some distance from the shore, was suddenly attacked by a large medusa, or galley fish, which so clogged his movements that he was in imminent danger of being drowned, and it was with difficulty ho disencumbered himself so iar as to admit of his diving, by which he freed himself for a moment fiotu his unwonted assailant. Unfortunately, howthe fear of a sudden and honible þÿoption. ever, on rising to the surface, he again came in contact with the animal, which this time began to sink along with him, and had it not been for the assistance of a fisherman, who, attracted by Ins cries, rowed hastily to the rescue, the result might very possibly have been fatal. As it is, he was for some lime confined to bed, and is still suffering from the feverish effect produced by the stings received in his strange encounter. This accident is the more worthy of notice from the size of the medusa, which is rarely found so large in these latitudes; being, so far as ihe observer's agitation would permit him to judge, at least six feet in circumference. þÿ Glasgow Ilerald.
